newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major makes "get rich with us" pitch.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major makes "get rich with us" pitch.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major, shrugging off grim opinion poll news, on Friday put plans for widening share ownership at the heart of his Conservative party's programme for the coming election.
He unveiled detailed proposals to create a "popular capitalism for the 21st century" by encouraging broader share ownership and more flexible private pensions.

"In the 1980s and 1990s we set the economy free. Now we must offer people more freedom over decisions that affect their lives. It will be a new era of more opportunity, wider choice and more personal ownership of assets," Major declared.
"Our aim is for everyone to have a People's Share in our enterprise economy," he told a news conference.

An opinion poll in Friday's Times newspaper suggested Major would not get the chance to implement what he called an ambitious agenda that would be "radical in improving people's lives, but offer stability to the Nation".
The MORI poll showed the main opposition Labour party's lead had risen by four points since early December to 55 percent. The government's support stayed static at 30 percent.
The gap is now 25 percentage points. No British party has ever reversed a lead of this size in less than four months, the time left to the last possible date for the election of May 22.

But Major, in confident mood, dismissed the survey as "complete rubbish". He said the Conservatives' own polling painted a very different picture and predicted the party would go on to win an unprecedented fifth election in a row.
Major's deputy, Michael Heseltine, was even more forthright.
Speaking in Glasgow, he said the mood of the country was changing and forecast the Conservatives would romp home at the election with a majority of 60 seats.
At the 1992 election, Major won an overall majority of 21 in the 651-seat House of Commons and a majority over Labour of 64.
The number of Britons who own shares has trebled to around 10 million since the Conservatives came to power in 1979.

Millions more will become shareholders for the first time in 1997 when a number of big building societies, which provide the bulk of Britain's home loans, become publicly quoted companies and hand out free shares to their savers and borrowers.
Major said he wanted to reinforce the trend by changing tax rules so big companies have an incentive to give free shares to staff who invest in employee share ownership schemes.

He hoped that by the turn of the century more than half of the employees of Britain's largest companies would own shares or options in their companies. "It's a way of building a people's share in the country's future as our economy grows," he said.
Major also announced plans to make personal pension schemes more flexible and to cut the local taxes paid by small businessmen, whom the Conservatives see as their natural allies.
He refused point blank to give any clues about when he will call the election.

"I will pick my own time, I will do it in my own way and I'm giving you no nods, no winks. And if you pick up nods and winks from anybody else, let me tell you now you are safe to ignore them -- because at the moment they don't know and I do."
